questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Strange foods eaten in countries like Thailand and Colombia
How to make healthy green smoothies at home
Why many ponds and lakes are becoming polluted
Whether microalgae could be good for us and the planet
questions.why: Neil says they'll ask whether eating algae might be better for our health and the planet's health.

questions.q: What is the strangest food Neil has eaten?
options: Pond scum from a lake in Wales
Fried stick insect and ants
Raw fish at a sushi restaurant
Spirulina pasta with green sauce
questions.why: He says he tried fried stick insect in Thailand and ants from Colombia.

questions.q: Why are microalgae like spirulina and chlorella good for us?
options: They are full of proteins, vitamins and antioxidants
They contain lots of natural sugar to give you energy
They help you sleep better and feel less stressed
They have no calories at all, so they help you diet
questions.why: Sam says they are packed full of proteins, vitamins and antioxidants.

questions.q: What helped make microalgae popular recently, according to Sam?
options: Doctors prescribing it to patients as a medicine
A big government health campaign on television
Drinks companies selling colourful smoothies
Famous chefs using it in recipes on TV shows
questions.why: She says the trend has been promoted partly by big drinks companies selling brightly coloured smoothies.

questions.q: How is spirulina now being used in cooking?
options: Only as a healthy drink, mixed with fruit juice
As a natural sweetener in cakes and biscuits
As a green colour for bread and pizza bases
In hot dogs and meatballs, and instead of eggs
questions.why: Neil says it's used in hot dogs and meatballs and as a substitute for eggs in pasta and mayonnaise.

questions.q: What problem does Professor Alison Smith describe?
options: More people, while farmland is becoming stretched
People refusing to eat enough fresh vegetables
Too much food being wasted by shops and families
Farmers using too many chemicals on their crops
questions.why: She says the world's population is increasing and land available for agriculture is becoming stretched.

questions.q: What does 'sustainable intensification' of agriculture aim to do?
options: Use a lot more land for farming around the world
Replace most farmers with machines and robots
Grow more food without harming nature or using new land
Make food more expensive so people waste less
questions.why: Sam says it means increasing food production without damaging the environment or using new land.

questions.q: Why does Professor Smith suggest microalgae could be produced in cities and towns?
options: City people eat more of it
They don't need open land to grow
It is cheaper to transport
Cities have cleaner water
questions.why: She says they could be produced in cities because they don't need the open landscape to be grown.
